sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: right versus left turn position, two-point versus three-point turnabouts, DDI versus RCUT, roundabout yielding and school bus road types
Confusable pairs among turn positions, turnabout types, special interchange designs, roundabout yielding and the school bus stopping rules, followed by continuation facts; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A01
Once a turn is complete, speed up smoothly to a suitable speed, check that your turn signal has switched off and keep track of traffic behind you. [A01]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty low.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A02
Right turns start from the right-most part of your lane and left turns from the left-most part, so the side of the lane matches the direction of the turn. [A02]
Why it matters: group turning; confusable right turn position versus left turn position.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A02
Where more than one lane turns, pick and enter the lane you will turn from and stay in that same lane until the turn is finished. [A02]
Why it matters: group turning; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A03
A two-point turnabout relies on a driveway or alley, while a three-point turn must be done without using a side street or driveway at all. [A03]
Why it matters: group turnabouts; confusable two-point versus three-point.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A03
The reverse two-point turnabout ends with a shift to drive, a check both ways and, if clear, a signal and a left turn into the proper lane. [A03]
Why it matters: group turnabouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A03
The forward two-point turnabout ends by backing slowly while turning the wheel fully right, then straightening, stopping, shifting to drive, cancelling the right signal and moving forward once centered in the nearest lane. [A03]
Why it matters: group turnabouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A03
When the street is busy, circling an entire city block is better than attempting a three-point turnabout. [A03]
Why it matters: group turnabouts; confusable busy street versus quiet two-lane road.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A05
You need a gap big enough to get all the way across the road, or to turn into the proper lane and build up to a suitable speed. [A05]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A05
Never assume another driver will share space with your vehicle or leave you any extra room. [A05]
Why it matters: group intersections; difficulty low.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A05
In a DDI, cross street traffic is shifted to the left side of the road between the signalized crossovers, so left turns onto or off the ramps do not conflict with traffic from other directions. [A05]
Why it matters: group interchanges; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A06
Besides cutting the number of conflicts, the DDI also lowers how severe those conflicts are. [A06]
Why it matters: group interchanges; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec09-R12 | anchor: A06
An RCUT turns a cross street left or through movement into a right turn followed by a U-turn at a median opening, and it can be controlled by a signal, a stop sign, or a merge or yield sign. [A06]
Why it matters: group interchanges; confusable RCUT versus DDI.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec09-R13 | anchor: A06
RCUT intersections reduce potential conflict points and increase safety. [A06]
Why it matters: group interchanges; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec09-R14 | anchor: A07
At a roundabout the entering driver is the one who yields, and the vehicles already circulating keep the right-of-way. [A07]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; confusable entering versus circulating traffic.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-R15 | anchor: A08
Either red or amber flashing lights on a stopped or stopping school bus, or its extended stop arm, mean you must stop. [A08]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable red versus amber lights.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-R16 | anchor: A09
On a multi-lane highway a driver meeting a school bus from the other direction is not covered by the stopping rule, while on a two-lane road every driver must stop. [A09]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable two-lane versus multi-lane.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0083]
